newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Singapore has taste for Australia crayfish.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Singapore has taste for Australia crayfish.

text.p: Under a searing sun, Jeffrey Teo mused about the diminutive lobster-like crayfish breeding in shallow ponds on his fish farm in the northwestern corner of Singapore.
"Their flesh is harder than prawn, but tender like lobster," he told Reuters.
The fish farm, spread over several hectares of the crowded island's rare open country, breeds redclaw freshwater lobster from Australia and ornamental fish.
Some of the male redclaws plucked out of holding tanks reared up on their hind legs and waved their claws menacingly in the air. At the bottom of one tank, hundreds of fry swam around lazily.

Singapore, population three million people, imports most of its food. The tiny city-state constantly seeks ways to maximise production such as the cultivation of plants which need little water, or the development of species like the redclaw which can be adapted to local conditions.

The city has always expressed a keen interest in maintaining some kind of farm sector and encourages research to develop ways to mass-produce food by using high-technology methods, although it will always be a net food importer.
LOCAL SCHOOL GIVES REDCLAW BREEDING A START
The Ngee Ann Polytechnic initiated the breeding of the redclaw in Singapore a few years ago. The institution has been teaching its students the rudiments of aqua-farming over the past few years.
"We were looking for something which may not be Singaporean which we can culture and breed," Sushila Chang, the head of Ngee Ann's Biotechnology Department, said in an interview.
"When I saw the redclaw, it seemed like a viable product to bring back to Singapore. I tasted the redclaw. It's like lobster," she added.
The only problem researchers had to overcome was that the redclaw came from Australian waters where the average temperature is much cooler than in tropical Singapore.

"We found they could actually tolerate our water temperature, our longer daylight period. The next step was to breed them to close the whole life cycle," said Alex Chang, who became executive director of the Redclaw Lobster Research Pte Ltd.
Teo said breeding the redclaw was not too difficult.
"They're very hardy creatures because basically, they're scavengers. They're bottom dwellers," he said.
Alex Chang said the redclaw could be harvested in six months and that some could grow to weigh 200 grams.
TASTE TEST GIVES LOCAL REDCLAW THUMBS UP
Seeking the thumbs up from diners, the researchers organised a tasting session last year among Singapore restaurant owners.
"We got them to compare the redclaw with the rock lobster. There were 21 of them and the majority...preferred the redclaw to the lobster in terms of texture," Sushila Chang said.
Alex Chang said interest from Singapore breeders eager to supply the city state's restaurants was high.
He said the researchers will be holding a seminar in July to instruct local breeders on how to raise the redclaw.
His group has already interviewed some 80 restaurants which said they would probably need about eight kilograms (17.6 pounds) of redclaw daily.
"If you manage the pond well, the returns are very high," Alex Chang said, adding one of their plans in the future is to expand production to supply consumers throughout Southeast and Northeast Asia.

He hopes the industry will take off in Singapore and that most breeders will be up and running before the three-month festive season lasting from Christmas in December to the Chinese Lunar New Year in February.
"There are a lot of interested farmers who want to grow redclaw," he said.
Longer-term, Alex Chang is optimistic demand for the redclaw will take off.
"There is big demand worldwide for redclaw," he said, adding that most of the supply was winding up on plates in Hong Kong and Japan where the demand for premium seafood was very high.
